backlinks.why: Gives structural balance and status evidence for signed networks, which bears on whether balance-based partitioning is a reasonable model of signed ties.
Signed link prediction. It covers the negative-tie question the co-appearance and reference layer needs, which Zareie's unsigned similarity cannot answer.
Tang reuses Leskovec et al.'s 16 weighted signed-triad features and signed-link setting, then extends them to the case where no negative links are observed.
Both argue that the sign or type of a relationship changes what a tie predicts, which is the issue behind the system's signed member-reference layer.
Trust-aware IM needs signed edges. Leskovec gives the method for predicting positive and negative links that such a kernel would need.

Uses structural balance on signed online networks to predict edge signs. It is the link-level counterpart to Aref and Neal's global frustration partition, relevant to the system's LLM-signed mention edges.

extraction.title: The Kernel of Truth in Text-Based Personality Assessment: A Meta-Analysis of the Relations Between the Big Five and the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)
extraction.venue: Psychological Bulletin, 148(11-12), 843-868. Correction to metadata hint: the hint said 2024; the PDF gives 2022 (received April 8, 2022; accepted November 2, 2022).
extraction.coverage: Read the full extracted text (all 4,110 lines, front matter through the reference list and receipt dates). Full coverage of the abstract, introduction, method, results (Tables 2-6 and Figure 3), discussion, limitations, conclusion and references. The paper contains no content on lobbying, legislators, networks, path-finding, allocation, or persuasion/turnout. Elections appear only as one included study task (Abe, 2018, reflection on U.S. elections; Table 2). Text measurement is covered in depth (LIWC closed-vocabulary method). Paul's markup: no files were listed for this PDF, and a search of /_annots for the document hash 694a803d85d2 returned no matches, so no markup was read or reported. Page numbers come from the running heads in the text dump and may be off by one in places; section and table locations are exact.
extraction.research_question: Do self-reported and observer-reported Big Five traits correlate with the 52 LIWC categories shared across LIWC2001, LIWC2007 and LIWC2015 (cue validity and cue utilization)? Which categories form a "kernel of truth" that both self- and observer-reports link to? Do 10 study, sample and task moderators explain heterogeneity in these effects? (Introduction, pp. 843-847.)
extraction.theory: Brunswik's (1955) lens model (cue validity vs cue utilization); Realistic Accuracy Model (Funder, 1995, 2012) for the kernel-of-truth idea; Self-Other Knowledge Asymmetry model (Vazire, 2010), which predicts observer reports will show larger effects for overt behavior such as verbal behavior; Trait Activation Theory (Tett and Guterman, 2000; Tett et al., 2021), used for predictions on language formality and task synchronicity; "words as attention" account of word use (Tausczik and Pennebaker, 2010).
extraction.data: 31 eligible samples from 26 studies (k = 31 samples, 26 studies), total N = 85,724 participants. Unit of analysis: sample/study-level correlations between Big Five trait scores and LIWC category scores. Cue validity: 26 self-report samples (Table 3 note reports k = 25, n = 83,243-84,084 for the analysed effects; Schwartz et al., 2013 alone has n = 72,809). Cue utilization: 5 observer-report samples (Table 3 note: n = 1,637). Mean age 27.96 years (SD 10.50) for cue validity samples; 23.66 (SD 5.52) for cue utilization. Text length >40 words required. Period: literature searched September 8-10, 2020, from 1999 onward (LIWC publication year). Eligible: healthy English-speaking adults; LIWC2022 excluded because it was published after the search. Screening: 691 database records plus 22 additional records; 429 abstracts screened; 124 full texts; 26 studies included (Figure 2, p. 849). Missing data: 12% of values imputed (see method).
extraction.method: PRISMA-reported systematic review followed by meta-analysis (random-effects model, R package "meta"). Effect size: Pearson r, Fisher z transformation and back-transformation; Spearman rho converted to r for one study. Corrected effects (rho) disattenuated for personality-measure reliability only (Cronbach alpha for self-reports; ICC for observer reports); LIWC categories not corrected. Missing effect sizes (12% of values) imputed with a self-devised "mean minus 1" rule (sum of available effects plus zeros, divided by k-1); analyses based on this rule (pp. 847-849). Heterogeneity: Cochran Q, I2, tau. Publication bias: Egger's test on uncorrected, nonimputed data. Moderators (five categorical: LIWC version, written-spoken, formality, synchronicity, sample composition; five continuous: sample size, text length, age, percentage women, publication year) tested with meta-regression. Explained variance per trait: meta-analytic linear regression of each trait on all LIWC categories in lavaan, using a 52-category weighted average correlation matrix from 14 studies (n = 6,405) and the harmonic mean n. Content vs function words analysed separately, using narrow categories only to avoid double counting. Two coders per study (first author coded all; four research assistants coded a quarter each).
extraction.identification: None in the econometric sense. This is a correlational meta-analysis. Cue validity is the correlation between self-reports and LIWC categories; cue utilization is the correlation between observer reports and LIWC categories; the "kernel of truth" is the set of categories significant in the same direction for both (Figure 1). The authors explicitly state that "valid cues" does not mean "true" personality.
extraction.scope: Population: healthy adults writing or speaking English (mostly students and general-population samples, US-centric social media). Era: studies from 1999 to 2020, LIWC2001, LIWC2007 and LIWC2015 only. Instrument scope: the 52 LIWC categories shared by these versions; Big Five (plus HEXACO Emotionality/Agreeableness treated as Big Five, one study). HEXACO Honesty-Humility not reported (single study). Text types: blogs, Facebook/Twitter posts, essays, dreams, interviews, daily speech (EAR), chats. Results are English-specific (p. 861).

measures: LIWC (LIWC2001, LIWC2007, LIWC2015): 52 categories shared across versions; word count, dictionary, words >6 letters, function-word and affect categories, and others (Table 1)
Big Five traits via self-report inventories (BFI-44, TIPI-10, IPIP-20/50/100/300, NEO-FFI, BFAS-100, HEXACO-PI-R; Table 2) and observer ratings (acquaintances, strangers, Facebook-based ratings)
Effect size: Pearson r (Fisher z pooled), corrected to rho for personality reliability (Cronbach alpha or ICC)
Explained variance R2 (%) per trait from meta-analytic regression across LIWC categories
Heterogeneity: Cochran Q, I2, tau; publication bias: Egger test
limitations: Corrected effects are probably underestimates: LIWC categories were not disattenuated for their reliability (authors argue they are formative measures; Limitations, p. 860).
Cue utilization rests on only k = 5 samples (vs 26 for cue validity), so categorical moderators could not be tested for it and the kernel of truth is probably underestimated (p. 861).
The cue-validity pool is dominated by Schwartz et al. (2013), n = 72,809 (the authors ran analyses with and without it).

12% of effect-size and moderator values were missing; missingness was non-random (non-significant effects were often unreported). The authors used a self-devised 'mean minus 1' imputation, which they admit may distort true effects (pp. 847-849).
Observer reports were mostly zero-acquaintance, and only one study used acquaintances; the acquaintance effect could not be tested (p. 861).
Several studies were small, and the authors note only large effects reach significance in small samples (p. 862).
Test-retest reliability was not used, because repeating verbal tasks can change responses (p. 860).
Results are English-specific, and LIWC has not been designed for personality assessment; Table 7 comparisons use each method's best category and are post hoc (footnote 9, p. 859).
Language formality and synchronicity are broad classifications, which may have attenuated situational moderation (p. 858).
Honesty-Humility is not covered (single study, Holtrop et al., 2019).
Egger's test flagged many cue-validity effects; the authors argue this reflects small-study effects rather than publication bias, which is a judgment call (p. 854).

summary_md:
Koutsoumpis et al. (Psychological Bulletin, 2022; the vault slug says 2024, the PDF says 2022) pooled 31 samples (N = 85,724). They correlated Big Five scores with the 52 LIWC categories shared by LIWC2001, 2007 and 2015.

**Self-reports (cue validity), 26 samples.** Effects are small. The strongest correlations run |rho| .08-.14, and all 52 categories together explain about 5.1% of trait variance.

**Observer ratings (cue utilization), only 5 samples (n = 1,637).** Effects are larger: |rho| .18-.39, with R2 averaging 38.5%.

**Overlap.** Only 20 of 260 trait-by-category markers agree in direction for both self and observer reports. The paper calls this the "kernel of truth". Examples: swear words, anger and negative emotion for low Conscientiousness and low Agreeableness, and negative emotion for low Emotional Stability.

**Other results.** Heterogeneity is nearly universal: 96% of self-report effects and 82% of observer effects. Formal settings weaken some markers, for example Agreeableness with swear words is -.07 formal vs -.14 informal. Spoken text carries much more Extraversion signal through word count than written text (.23 vs .03). LIWC also trails other computer methods (.10 vs .27-.31).

**Why it matters for Melange.** The system's lexical Big Five (`big5_traits.py`) is this closed-vocabulary method applied to formal congressional speech. It uses short published-exemplar word lists, not licensed LIWC dictionaries. The paper sets a low ceiling on how much true trait signal such rates can carry. That supports four existing choices: the brain's reading that the RKH convergence (CV mean .350) is inflated by shared method, retiring the lexical basis from the receptivity layer, square-root token shrinkage, and keeping status labels on any external claim.

The paper also gives a direction check for the active SMOreg weights, and some of them point the opposite way. Finally, observer-panel passes need care. The paper says plainly that valid cues are not the same as true personality, so convergence with the Senate expert panels may partly reflect raters using the same cues the text model uses (utilization), not validity.

bearings.paper_claim: Self-reported Big Five correlate with LIWC categories at most |rho| .08-.14. All 52 categories together explain a mean R2 of 5.07% of self-reported trait variance (narrow categories; k = 25, n about 83-84k, dominated by Schwartz et al. 2013, n = 72,809). Heterogeneity is significant in 96% of these effects. LIWC's average best-category r of .10 trails other computer methods (.27-.31).

It combines them with linear weights; the essays-fitted SMOreg weights are active when the json file is present, then refit to RKH. Reported held-out CV vs RKH has mean .350 (E .510). Congressional floor speech and interviews are formal and partly staff-written. The paper shows formality attenuates markers (Agreeableness-swear -.14 informal vs -.07 formal). The system uses short exemplar lists (swear = 'damn hell crap'), not licensed LIWC dictionaries, so category equivalence is unverified. Read the paper as an upper bound on true trait signal from closed-vocabulary rates. A text-vs-RKH convergence of .35 therefore cannot be read as trait validity, which agrees with the brain's method-shared caveat.

gaps_exposed: The lexical reader has no licensed LIWC dictionary: categories are short exemplar lists (swear = 3 words) plus the Empath overlay. The paper's effect sizes are for LIWC dictionaries, and the system has no check that its categories are equivalent.

There is no formality or genre moderator in the lexical model. The paper shows formality and spoken vs written mode change effect sizes (Agreeableness-swear -.14 vs -.07; Extraversion-word count spoken .23 vs written .03). The system pools floor, interview and social text and has already seen genre transfer fail for N.

No sign audit of the fitted SMOreg weights against literature kernel directions. ES on first-person singular and E on positive emotion run opposite to the paper, and ES on negative emotion is near zero.

No open-vocabulary or embedding benchmark: the paper's Table 7 puts other computer methods at r .27-.31 against LIWC's .10 for self-reports. The system's alternative LLM reader is display-only and failed its behavioral diagonal (+0.064).
No cue-validity vs cue-utilization distinction in the validation framing: observer-panel convergence (E, A) is not separated from shared-stereotype cue use.
flags: Metadata: the vault slug and hint say 2024. The paper is Psychological Bulletin 2022, 148(11-12), 843-868, doi 10.1037/bul0000381.

Documentation drift: the component brief says affective_n = z(LIWC) + z(LLM). The live code, emit_affective_n.py:39-43, says LIWC is only the convergent-validity anchor since round-7b, and the measure is the E-residualized, party-controlled LLM affective-N.

The active SMOreg weights (fec/liwc/mairesse_smoreg.json:20, :43, :51) give E a negative weight on positive emotion, ES a positive weight on first-person singular, and ES a near-zero weight on negative emotion, against the paper's directions. This is a multivariate-suppression caveat, not proof of error. UNVERIFIED single-path analysis (DE-062).

Do not quote the RKH held-out CV (.350, E .510) as trait validity. RKH is itself Mairesse-LIWC text-derived, and the paper's 5% ceiling on self-report variance makes method-shared inflation the likely explanation.
Do not read observer-panel passes as trait accuracy. The paper says valid or utilized cues do not mean 'true' personality, and its observer evidence rests on k = 5 mostly zero-acquaintance samples.
No brain wording rule is triggered: the paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, and makes no LDA, reciprocity or influence claims.
paul_alignment:
Paul calls Ramey's closed-vocabulary approach "dated but foundational" and asks for frameworks specific to each venue. Birkenmaier's highlights call Ramey's SVM outdated and unvalidated. This meta-analysis backs both points with numbers. Closed-vocabulary categories explain only about 5% of self-reported trait variance, and venue matters: formality, spoken vs written, and heterogeneity in 96% of effects. So the evidence agrees with his skepticism and with his call for venue-specific frameworks.

His notes are stale relative to the system. They do not record three things:
- The pre-registered nomological test already indicted the lexical Big5 for behavioral prediction, and the receptivity layer now defaults to a behavioral basis (receptivity_layer.py:59-64).
- N now comes from an E-residualized LLM reader, with LIWC only as an anchor.
- RKH convergence is method-shared.

The paper does not support his endorsement of LLM trait reading directly, because it does not test LLMs. It only shows that non-LIWC computer methods reach r of about .27-.31. The system's own LLM reader has not cleared its behavioral bar.

related.why: Ramey et al. apply LIWC/Mairesse closed-vocabulary trait scoring to congressional speech, the RKH source the system calibrates to. This meta-analysis sets the ceiling on how much true trait signal that method can carry.
Pennebaker's 'words as attention' account and the LIWC category design are the theoretical and instrumental base the meta-analysis evaluates.
A parallel meta-analysis of predicting the Big Five from social-media footprints. Its larger pooled effects contrast with LIWC-only effects and frame the open- vs closed-vocabulary gap.

A Twitter-based study of Emotional Stability linguistic markers. It bears on the paper's six ES kernel markers and on the system's affective-N anchor.

Meta-analysis of LIWC-Big Five validity. Together with Rice & Zorn's LIWC benchmark shortfall, it bears on the system's demotion of LIWC to an anchor in affective N.
A meta-analysis of LIWC-Big Five relations, which bounds what the closed-vocabulary features the survey treats as baseline (and the system's lexical reader) can recover.
A meta-analysis of LIWC-Big Five correlations. Together with the BFI-2 cross-rater and cross-instrument convergence figures, it brackets what text-to-trait convergence can reasonably reach.
A meta-analysis of LIWC-Big Five correlations. It gives realistic, small magnitudes for the LIWC features this paper proposes, and bears on the closed-vocabulary weights in big5_traits.py.

meta.title: Optimal Targeting in Fundraising
meta.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2103.10251v3 [econ.EM], 29 Sep 2021 (dated September 30, 2021 on the title page). No journal appears in the text. AEA RCT Registry ID AEARCTR-0007581. The metadata hint matches the text.

extraction.title: Optimal Targeting in Fundraising
extraction.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2103.10251v3 [econ.EM], 29 Sep 2021 (dated September 30, 2021 on the title page). No journal appears in the text. AEA RCT Registry ID AEARCTR-0007581. The metadata hint matches the text.
extraction.document_type: Working paper / arXiv preprint with online appendix (Appendices A-I)
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 4,079 lines of the file, including main text (pp. 1-34), references (pp. 34-39) and Online Appendix A-I (pp. 1-21). No Paul markup exists for this item (no markup files were supplied), so paul_markup is empty.
extraction.research_question: Can a charity raise more net donations (donations minus fundraising cost) by targeting an unconditional gift (small Dürer postcards mailed with a solicitation letter) to a subset of potential donors, using causal machine learning to learn an optimal targeting rule from a randomized field experiment, and does that rule generalize? Theory: charities face costly fundraising and donor overhead aversion (Rose-Ackerman 1982; Name-Correa and Yildirim 2013; Gneezy et al. 2014); the optimal rule targets "net donors" whose expected additional donation exceeds the marginal cost; heterogeneous motives (altruism, warm glow, reciprocity, sequential reciprocity) make gift effects heterogeneous across individuals.
extraction.data: Natural field experiment in 2014 with a Catholic Church fundraiser in a German urban area (26% of residents are church members). Unit: individual church member (donor). Sample of 19,779 individuals: warm list (previous donors) N=2,354 (1,180 gift, 1,174 control); cold list (never donors) N=17,425 (2,283 gift, 15,142 control). Randomization stratified on list, gender, household type, quintiles of predicted baseline giving and age quintiles. Outcomes: donation amount in euro in the first year after the experiment (2015) and the first two years; donation dummy; net donation (donation minus gift variable cost, 1.16 euro). Covariates: (a) administrative records (gender, marital status, age, residency, donation history 2006-2015, per the text) and (b) Google Maps geospatial counts within 300 m (restaurants, supermarkets, medical, cultural facilities, churches) plus distances to station, city hall, main church and airport, travel time and elevation. External validity: 2015 follow-up experiment on a new warm-list sample (text says N=3,616; Table G.2 says 3,612), 50% gift probability; the 2015 sample is matched to 2014 by caliper propensity-score matching (radius 0.1). The text states donation records run 2006-2015 while also saying two post-experiment years were observed; the second year's dates are not reconciled in the text.
extraction.method:
Potential-outcomes framework. CATE delta(x) and ATE identified under stratified randomization and SUTVA (Appendix B). Outcome-model/propensity nuisance estimation: logit for propensity, OLS for outcome regressions (Table D.1), combined into an augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW) score (Eq. 3-4). Optimal targeting rule estimated directly via Athey and Wager (2021) empirical welfare maximization, using exact policy-learning trees of Zhou, Athey and Wager (2018) with search depth two (policytree R package). Gains evaluated by 20-fold cross-validation of out-of-sample net donations versus all-gift, no-gift and random-gift benchmarks. Descriptive heterogeneity: sorted-effects approach (Chernozhukov, Fernandez-Val and Luo 2018) with multiplier-bootstrap bands, plus best linear predictor test with causal forest (Chernozhukov et al. 2020). Data-type ablations (socioeconomic, donation history, geospatial, combinations). Sensitivity to depth one and three exact trees, CART (fixed and cross-validated depth), weighted logit (baseline and flexible), logit lasso, classification forest; nuisance robustness via population propensity and cross-fitted lasso (Tables I.1-I.4). Identification of the targeting gain does not require identifying the causal effect of each characteristic; trees indicate correlations only.
Identification strategy: random assignment of the gift within strata (Zi), exogenous of potential outcomes conditional on Zi, 0 < p(z) < 1; heterogeneity variables Xi are not needed for identification.
extraction.scope: Population: church members in one German urban area, targeted by one Catholic Church fundraiser with an annual solicitation mailing, split into warm (past donors) and cold (never donors) lists. Institution: a single religious charity; religious giving is the largest private giving category in Germany (about 35% of private giving per the text, citing Deutscher Spendenrat 2016). Era: 2014 treatment with 2015 (and second-year) outcomes; 2015 follow-up experiment on warm list. The paper states the findings may be specific to the setting.

key_findings.finding: Gift ATE on donations (first year): warm list +1.21 to +1.24 euro, not significant. Net of the 1.16 euro gift cost: +0.05 to +0.08 euro, not significant. Cold list ATE +0.19 euro (significant); net of cost -0.97 euro per donor, so the all-gift rule loses money in the cold list.
key_findings.numbers: warm ATE 1.21-1.24 (SE 1.15-1.25); warm net 0.05-0.08; cold ATE 0.19 (SE 0.07-0.10); cold net -0.97 (SE 0.07-0.10); preferred AIPW warm ATE 1.22, net 0.06

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity: sorted effects show substantial individual variation in warm-list gift effects; 45% of warm-list individuals have estimated effects above the 1.16 euro cost. Effects range from +17.99 euro (95th percentile responders) to -11.59 euro (5th percentile). In the cold list, effects exceed cost only above the 92nd percentile and are small.
key_findings.numbers: warm: 45% above cost; 5th pct -11.59 euro; responsive individuals +17.99 euro; cold: 5th pct -0.73, 95th pct +1.38 euro

key_findings.finding: Best linear predictor test with causal forest detects significant effect heterogeneity in the warm list and none in the cold list.
key_findings.location: Section 5.2 and Table E.3 (p.21; Appendix p.12)
key_findings.numbers: warm heterogeneity loading 0.959* (SE 0.710); cold 0.511 (SE 1.069)

key_findings.finding: Warm list optimal rule (cross-validated out-of-sample): gift is assigned to 33% of warm-list individuals; expected net donations 17.61 euro, which is 2.14 euro (13.8%) above all-gift, 2.20 euro (14.3%) above no-gift, and 2.17 euro (14.1%) above random-gift, all significant.
key_findings.numbers: share treated 0.33; net donation 17.61 euro (SE 0.97); vs all-gift 2.14*** (0.82); vs no-gift 2.20*** (0.81); vs random 2.17*** (0.58)

key_findings.finding: Secondary outcomes (warm list): donation probability in first year is +0.025 (significant at 5%) vs no-gift, with no significant difference from the all-gift rule; net donations over two years are 32.94 euro, +2.33 vs all-gift and +3.75 vs no-gift, so the gains persist and there is no evidence of pull-forward.
key_findings.numbers: donation probability 1st year 0.503; vs no-gift 0.025**; two-year net donations 32.94 euro; +2.33* vs all-gift; +3.75*** vs no-gift; two-year probability 0.582

key_findings.finding: Cold list optimal rule assigns the gift to only 1.4% of cold-list individuals. Expected net donation 0.15 euro, essentially equal to no-gift (-0.005, not significant), and significantly above all-gift (0.97 euro) and random-gift (0.48 euro). The paper concludes the gift should not be sent to cold-list individuals at all.
key_findings.numbers: share treated 0.014; net donation 0.15***; vs all-gift 0.97*** (0.10); vs no-gift -0.005 (0.012); vs random 0.48*** (0.05)

key_findings.finding: Warm-list targeted (net donor) vs non-targeted (net receiver) characteristics: targeted donors gave more before the experiment (average 4.10 vs 3.90 prior donations; 130.98 vs 123.39 euro total prior donations), live at lower elevation (308.66 vs 321.38 m), and have more restaurants, churches and cultural facilities nearby. Socioeconomic differences are small. Sample: 787 targeted vs 1,567 non-targeted.
key_findings.numbers: elevation std diff 157.80; cultural facilities 0.240 vs 0.050 (std diff 32.27); female share 0.507 vs 0.539 (std diff 6.46)

key_findings.finding: Cold-list targeted vs non-targeted: targeted individuals live closer to city hall, main station and airport, have fewer restaurants nearby (5.48 vs 10.40), and are more often female (0.558 vs 0.503) and single (0.713 vs 0.642). Sample: 251 targeted vs 17,174 non-targeted.
key_findings.numbers: distance to city hall 1.364 vs 2.816 km (std diff 103.02); restaurants 5.482 vs 10.40 (std diff 57.08)

key_findings.finding: Data needed: the warm-list rule using only geospatial data (17.40 euro expected net donation, +1.92** vs all-gift, +1.98** vs no-gift) or only donation history (17.20 euro, +1.73** and +1.79**) performs about as well as the baseline (17.61 euro). Socioeconomic data alone do not beat the three benchmarks (15.71 euro; differences insignificant). Adding socioeconomic data does not improve the rules. Cold list: geospatial-only rule gives 0.15 euro, the same as the baseline.
key_findings.numbers: warm geospatial-only 17.40; donation-history-only 17.20; socioeconomic-only 15.71 with vs no-gift 0.27 (insignificant); cold geospatial-only 0.15 with vs no-gift -0.005

key_findings.finding: External validity over time: the 2014 rule applied to a caliper-matched 2015 warm-list sample (radius 0.1) yields 19.85 euro expected net donation, +2.64* vs all-gift and +2.30** vs no-gift, and 35.6% treated. Applied to the full 2015 sample it yields 17.16 euro with no significant gain over all-gift (-0.88) or no-gift (+0.45). The text says the 2015 average gift effect is 1.33 euro vs 0.08 in 2014.

Caliper sensitivity: the 2014 rule significantly beats no-gift up to a caliper radius of 0.25; beating all-gift is harder because the gift raises average net donations in the full 2015 sample. Above 0.1 the effects are no longer statistically significant but remain positive in expectation.
key_findings.location: Section 5.6 and Appendix H, Figure H.1 (p.31-32)
key_findings.numbers: significance against no-gift holds to caliper 0.25; radius 0.1 is the standard

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity: in the warm list, the baseline exact policy tree (depth 2) dominates the alternative estimators, which yield lower net donations. Depth-1 trees and flexible logit have the lowest performance. The cross-validated-depth CART is the only alternative that significantly beats both all-gift and no-gift (17.40 euro, +1.93** and +1.98**). In the cold list, logit lasso and cross-validated CART are 0.01 euro higher, but the no-gift conclusion holds.
key_findings.numbers: CV-CART warm 17.40 (+1.93 vs all-gift); flexible logit 16.28; depth-1 tree 15.05; cold logit lasso/CV-CART +0.01 euro

key_findings.finding: Nuisance-parameter robustness: using the population propensity score or cross-fitted logit-lasso nuisances gives essentially identical results (warm 17.63 and 17.35 euro expected net donation; cold 0.15 euro).
key_findings.numbers: population propensity: warm 17.63, +2.15***, +2.21***; cross-fitted lasso: warm 17.35, +1.85***, +1.79**

key_findings.finding: Example decision trees: the warm-list tree splits first on maximum prior donation (101.76 euro) and home elevation (313.55 m). The cold-list tree splits on number of restaurants within 300 m (5), distance to city hall (1.28 km) and distance to airport (3.06 km). The text warns that trees show correlations, not causal effects.
key_findings.location: Section 5.4 and Figure F.1 (p.26-27; Appendix p.13)
key_findings.numbers: warm leaves: gift 4.94 euro (N=758), 81.13 euro (N=48); cold leaf 21.44 euro (N=58)

measures: Donation amount in euro, first year after the experiment (2015), and cumulative first two years
Donation dummy (any donation), first year and first two years
Net donation = donation minus gift variable cost (1.16 euro for the gift treatment; letter costs 0.43 euro)
Expected net donation under a targeting rule P(pi), and excess net donation versus all-gift (Q1), no-gift (Q-1) and random-gift (QR) benchmarks
Share of individuals assigned the gift by the rule

limitations: Authors state that findings 'may well be specific to the setting' (one Catholic Church fundraiser, one German urban area, one annual letter with a folded-card gift).

The optimal targeting rule identifies the policy gain, not the causal effect of each characteristic; trees show correlations, and unobserved variables (e.g., income, willingness to give) may drive the heterogeneity (Section 5.4).
The gain estimates are cross-validated (K=20) rather than from a fresh holdout sample; external validity is tested only on one 2015 follow-up with warm-list individuals.

External validity holds only when the new sample is similar to the training sample: the 2014 rule works against no-gift up to caliper 0.25, but against all-gift only for similar samples; the full 2015 sample shows no significant gains (Table 8).

Cold-list results have far fewer treated individuals in the rule (1.4%, 251 individuals), and depth-three exact trees are infeasible in the cold list (Table I.2 note), so the cold-list tree comparison is limited.
Data scope: the authors use only covariates the charity can collect (administrative records and Google Maps data); richer data could change results (Section 5.5 and Conclusion).
Robustness checks use parametric nuisance estimators (logit and OLS); the authors note the AIPW estimator requires consistent and fast-converging nuisance estimators (Section 4.3).

Internal inconsistencies in the text: the 2015 follow-up sample is 3,616 in the text but 3,612 in Table G.2 and 1,806+1,806 in Table G.1; the Table 8 note cites an expected 17.01 euro while the table shows 19.85; the text says donation records cover 2006-2015 but also refers to two post-experiment years.

summary_md:
Cagala, Glogowsky, Rincke and Strittmatter ran a natural field experiment in 2014 with a Catholic Church fundraiser in one German city (N=19,779 church members). A small gift (postcards, cost 1.16 euro) was randomly assigned with the solicitation letter, stratified by warm list (past donors, N=2,354) and cold list (never donors, N=17,425). Sending the gift to everyone barely paid for itself on the warm list (net +0.06 euro, not significant) and lost money on the cold list (-0.97 euro per person). Gift effects varied widely across warm-list donors, from -11.59 to +17.99 euro between the 5th and 95th percentiles. The authors used AIPW scores and a depth-2 exact policy tree (Athey-Wager policy learning) to learn who should get the gift. Under 20-fold cross-validation, the rule sent the gift to 33% of the warm list and raised expected net donations by about 2.1-2.2 euro (about 14%) over all-gift, no-gift and random assignment. On the cold list the rule chose almost nobody (1.4%). Geospatial covariates alone did about as well as the full set of covariates. Applied to a new 2015 sample, the rule only helped where the 2015 donors closely resembled the 2014 donors (caliper match 0.1). On the full 2015 sample it showed no significant gain.

What this means for Paul's systems: a targeting rule for a costly treatment is only justified when it beats uniform and random benchmarks out of sample, and that requires randomized variation in the treatment. Melange's money allocators and Terrier's canvass potential score both target on heterogeneity that is assumed, through hand-set response curves, multipliers and weights. Neither is learned from a randomized assignment. The paper describes the experiment and benchmark test the system lacks. It does not validate any of the system's constants. Its setting (individual charitable donors) also differs from the system's targets: legislators for Melange, and voters for Terrier.

bearings.paper_claim: A targeting rule for a costly instrument earns its keep only when its out-of-sample net gain beats all-treat, no-treat and random benchmarks. The warm-list rule gained +2.14, +2.20 and +2.17 euro (about 14%, cross-validated). In the full 2015 sample the gain over all-gift and no-gift vanished (-0.88 and +0.45, not significant). Heterogeneity was identified only from randomized gift assignment (AIPW plus policy tree).
bearings.system_side: CELF greedy allocates a $2.5M pot in $500 chunks to maximize modeled winnability. Per-member returns come from the design-set saturating pflip money term, scaled by pressure_mult and the competitiveness multiplier. Greedy is certified optimal only within the model (fixed-state certificate). No realized-outcome comparison is made against uniform, random or no-spend allocation.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The transferable part is the evaluation design: benchmark-relative, net-of-cost gains measured on held-out units under randomized treatment. The effect sizes do not transfer, because the paper studies a 1.16-euro gift to German church donors in 2014-15, not PAC dollars to Members of Congress. FEC limits and the absence of randomization mean the system cannot directly replicate the paper's identification. Any optimizer gain stays model-internal (UNVERIFIED per DE-062) until outcomes are scored against a benchmark allocation.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-allocation#Joint CU budget optimizer|Joint CU budget optimizer]]

bearings.paper_claim: Where a treatment works better is an empirical CATE question. Even after detection with a causal forest (BLP loading 0.959 on the warm list, none on the cold list), the learned rule failed to carry over to a population that differed: no significant gain on the full 2015 sample, and significance only up to caliper 0.1 against all-gift. Trees show correlates, not the causal role of a covariate.
bearings.paper_location: Section 5.2, Table E.3; Section 5.4; Section 5.6 and Figure H.1
bearings.system_side: c = 1 + 1.0*exp(-max(lean,0)/5.0) scales effective dollars, assuming dollars buy more in competitive seats. Brain records it as owner judgment, uncalibrated (D-104..D-108), default ON.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper is about method, not legislators or PVI. It shows how heterogeneous dollar effectiveness would have to be established (randomized variation plus a heterogeneity test plus checks of transfer to a new population). It gives no evidence for or against the PVI shape. Do not cite it as support for c.

bearings.paper_claim: Responsiveness to a costly contact is heterogeneous and is not the same as baseline propensity. Warm-list gift effects ranged from -11.59 to +17.99 euro, and only 45% of warm-list donors exceeded cost. Cheap geospatial covariates (300 m counts, distances, elevation) learned a rule as good as the full set (17.40 vs 17.61 euro). Socioeconomic data alone did not beat the benchmarks (15.71 euro).
bearings.system_side: potential = (wp*(1-|2s-1|)*t + (1-wp)*s*(1-t))*(1+wi*i), with hand-set wp=wi=0.5. Persuasion and mobilization value are assumed from the support level and turnout propensity, not estimated contact effects. Knocked doors with saved results exist but are not used to learn response.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies to individual-level targeting of a costly contact, which is structurally closest to Terrier. It does not transfer the paper's numbers, because those come from charitable gifts rather than canvass persuasion or GOTV. A learned rule would need randomized contact assignment (for example a held-out control list per turf), not the saved walk results, which are selected on who was knocked. The paper also warns that a rule fit in one year or district may not carry over to the next.

bearings.paper_claim: Policy gains are identified from randomized assignment through the AIPW score, without needing to identify each covariate's causal effect. The paper's cross-validated gains were then checked against a new-year sample, where they held only for similar units.
bearings.system_side: The H1 and H2 contracts are explicitly limited to forecasting (claim_scope 'receptivity_forecast_only_not_spending_effects'). The system has no design that identifies the effect of spending or contact.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper shows the missing design: randomized treatment within strata. That is the precondition for upgrading the contract from forecasting to spending-effect evidence. This is feasible for Terrier contacts or CU outreach logs. It is not feasible for statutory PAC contributions to legislators. The paper used 20-fold CV rather than a single-look holdout, which is weaker than the system's discipline.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-validation#Prospective receptivity contract (H1-H2) and forecast ledger|Prospective receptivity contract (H1-H2) and forecast ledger]]

bearings.paper_claim: Treating everyone above a ranking (all-gift) can be net-negative or near zero (cold list -0.97 euro, warm list +0.06 euro). Ranking by baseline giving is not the same as ranking by response: targeted warm donors differed only modestly in prior giving (130.98 vs 123.39 euro).
bearings.system_side: Funds the top 133 of 533 members from a flat $2.0M pot in proportion to the blended influence score. The score ordering is assumed to equal funding priority, with no response or cost term.
bearings.code_ref: Moneyball Main Version - Blended.xlsx Blended Model col U (no Python producer; fec/apply_alloc_cap.py not applied)
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is conceptual. The paper's warning is that a level ranking (influence, past giving) is not an effect ranking. The magnitudes come from donors, not legislators. It supports asking that the proportional allocator be compared against a uniform or random benchmark. It does not show that the allocator is wrong.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-allocation#Workbook allocator (top-133 from fixed pot)|Workbook allocator (top-133 from fixed pot)]]

gaps_exposed: No randomized or held-out variation in any costly treatment (PAC dollars, outreach, canvass contact). Every response heterogeneity in the allocators and in Terrier is an owner-set prior, not an estimated CATE.
No benchmark-relative evaluation: neither the optimizer nor the workbook allocator reports realized, net-of-cost gain against all-fund, no-fund or random-fund allocations.

Terrier's untapped-potential score targets on support level and turnout propensity. It has no estimate of who responds to a knock, and saved walk results are selected (non-random), so they cannot identify response.

There is no check that a targeting rule carries over to a changed population (new Congress, new district, new cycle), which is the paper's 2015 caliper test. The paper's rule lost significance on the full new sample.
There is no test of which covariate families (cheap geospatial vs administrative vs socioeconomic) are sufficient for targeting, which matters for Terrier's vendor-field costs.
flags: Do not cite this paper as evidence that dollars buy more in competitive seats or that reciprocity holds. It studies charitable donors, not legislators, and reciprocity is NOT validated (D-104..D-108).

Any figure quoted from it must name its window and denominator. Examples: 2014 treatment with 2015 first-year outcomes; warm list N=2,354, of whom 787 were targeted; cold list N=17,425; the 2015 follow-up sample is 3,616 in the text and 3,612 in Table G.2 (an internal inconsistency).
The headline +14% gain is cross-validated in-sample (K=20). On the full 2015 sample, the gain over all-gift was not significant (-0.88 euro). Quote both, never the 14% alone.
Any agent-built Terrier or allocator benchmark inspired by this paper stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
The paper makes no SNA, LDA-edge or per-edge normalization argument, so the rejected-proposal flags do not apply.
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper, so no note is stale. It partly cuts against his ROI framing of money (flip-model and break-even positions): uniformly applied, the costly instrument barely covered its cost, and it paid only when targeted on response that had been learned from randomized data. It partly supports his joint-optimizer position that a learned policy should eventually replace hand-built greedy targeting. The paper's sense of 'learned', though, is causal policy learning from an RCT, not GCOMB-style learning over graphs. On Terrier, Paul highlighted the Kalla & Broockman canvass protocol. This paper adds the complementary point: who to contact should be estimated from randomized contact, not assumed from support level and turnout propensity.

related.why: Also estimates returns to targeting a persuasion treatment on heterogeneous effects versus a uniform message, which is the same benchmark-relative question in political persuasion.
Microtargeting persuasion experiment: tests whether tailoring a treatment to individual traits beats a uniform treatment, which parallels the paper's policy-tree versus all-gift comparison.

Randomized field experiment on a costly political instrument (contributions to obtain access). This is the kind of identification the paper says a targeting rule needs, and it concerns the system's actual target.
Shows that treatment effects (returns to moderation) depend on where voters are, the same heterogeneity-depends-on-population lesson as the paper's failure to carry over to the 2015 sample.
Agent-based proof of principle that micro-targeting beats broadcast; this paper supplies the field-experimental counterpart with real net-of-cost numbers.

extraction.title: Negative Link Prediction in Social Media
extraction.coverage: Read the full extracted text (1,523 lines, pages 87-96, abstract through references). Metadata hint confirmed: title, authors, WSDM 2015 and DOI match the text. No lobbying, elections, legislators, persuasion/turnout or text-measurement content appears in this paper. Figure 4 (cross-site generalization) and Figures 2, 3 and 5 are axis labels only in the extraction, so plotted values are not recoverable; only numbers stated in prose or tables are reported. No Paul markup files were supplied (the task listed none), so paul_markup is empty.
extraction.research_question: Can negative (distrust/foe) links be predicted in social media when no negative links are observed, using only positive links and content-centric user interactions (likes/dislikes, ratings, posted opinions)? (Abstract; Sec. 1; Sec. 2, Eq. 1: f: {Gp, A, O} -> Gn.)
extraction.theory: Balance theory (Heider; Cartwright and Harary) and status theory (Leskovec et al.) as structural constraints on signed triads, plus the empirical claim that negative interactions (disagreement/antagonism) correlate with negative links. The "enemies are close" pattern (negative-link pairs sit within a few hops in the positive network) motivates the features (Sec. 3.1-3.3).
extraction.data: Two sites with explicit trust/distrust or friend/foe links, used for analysis and ground truth. Epinions: 14,765 users, 272,513 positive links, 52,704 negative links, 612,321 posts, 6,937,986 positive opinions, 163,502 negative opinions. Slashdot: 7,275 users, 67,705 positive links, 20,851 negative links, 300,932 posts, 1,742,763 positive opinions, 42,260 negative opinions (Table 1, p. 89). Unit of analysis: ordered user pair. Imbalance of negative to missing pairs is 1:4131 (Epinions) and 1:2534 (Slashdot) (Sec. 4.1, p. 90). Collection period is not stated. Epinions opinions come from helpfulness ratings (>3 positive, <3 negative); Slashdot opinions come from MPQA-lexicon polarity of comments (Sec. 3, p. 88). Users with no positive or negative links were filtered out.
extraction.method: Descriptive analysis (shortest-path distributions, balance and status triad counts, a two-sample t-test and ratio curves), then a supervised classifier, NeLP. Labels: missing pairs are positive samples; negative samples come from pairs with negative interactions (Algorithm 1), refined by status-theory removals and additions, with reliability weights W = f(Nij) if Nij > 0, else r, where f(x) = 1 - 1/log(1+x) (Eq. 2; Sec. 4.1, 5.2). Features: 45 per pair (8 user features for each member, 7 pair features, 22 signed features including 16 weighted triads from Leskovec et al.) (Sec. 4.2). Model: soft-margin SVM with separate costs Cp (positives) and Cn (negatives), per-sample negative weights cj, and a balance-theory Laplacian regularizer weighted by Cb (Eqs. 4-6), solved in dual QP form with a kernel (Eqs. 7-15). Parameters: Cp=1, Cn=0.5, Cb=0.1 (Epinions); Cp=1, Cn=0.7, Cb=0.01 (Slashdot) (Sec. 5.2). Baselines: Random; sPath (predict negative for pairs at a fixed shortest-path length); negIn (predict negative for pairs with negative interactions); negInS (negIn refined by status-theory steps); NeLP-negIn (NeLP trained on negIn labels). Parameterized baselines are reported at their best setting (Sec. 5.2, p. 93).
extraction.identification_strategy: None in a causal sense. Prediction is framed as supervised classification with constructed (noisy) labels. Evidence for signal comes from a t-test and conditional ratios (Sec. 3.3). Generalization is checked by training on one site and testing on the other (Sec. 5.2, Fig. 4). Ablations remove components (Cn, cj, Cb) one at a time (Sec. 5.3, Tables 4-5) and vary Cb over {0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1} (Sec. 5.4, Fig. 5). The text does not describe the train/test split, folds, or how evaluation negatives were drawn.
extraction.scope: Population: online users of two platforms (Epinions product-review trust network; Slashdot technology-news friend/foe network). No institutional or regulatory setting. Era: not stated; the datasets are pre-2015 snapshots. Claims are limited to these two platforms and to pairs with at least one positive link or interaction. Generalization is tested only between these two sites.

key_findings.numbers: A trivial all-missing classifier can reach 99.99% accuracy in a sparse network (text example)

measures: Negative-class F1-measure (harmonic mean of precision and recall, Sec. 5.1)
Negative-class precision (the emphasized metric, Sec. 5.1)
Shortest-path length between ui and uj in the positive network (BFS; 'inf' if unreachable)
Share of negative-link pairs within k hops
Triad balance (four sign patterns, two balanced) and status-theory consistency
Pair-level count of negative interactions Nij
Ratio of pairs with negative links among pairs with at least K negative interactions
Two-sample t-test on negative-link indicators for interacting vs matched pairs
Relative F1 and precision change in ablations
Weighted in/out-degree and Jaccard coefficients on positive and negative links, plus 16 weighted triads (45 features total)
limitations: Negative labels are not observed. Training labels are constructed from negative interactions and status-theory refinement, and the paper says they are noisy, especially for negatives (Sec. 4.3, p. 91; Sec. 7, p. 95).
Negative links in Epinions and Slashdot serve only as ground truth for analysis and evaluation; the model itself does not use them (Sec. 3, p. 88).
Opinion labels are proxies: Epinions helpfulness ratings are thresholded at 3, and Slashdot comment polarity comes from the MPQA lexicon (Sec. 3, p. 88).
Severe class imbalance (1:4131 and 1:2534), so precision and F1 stay modest (best F1 0.3242 Epinions, 0.2441 Slashdot) (Sec. 4.1, Table 3).
Balance regularization uses only pairs at shortest-path length 2 plus the labeled sets, a simplification for scale (Sec. 4.3, p. 92).
Parameterized baselines are reported at their best setting, and NeLP parameters differ per site (Sec. 5.2, p. 93). The text gives no held-out tuning protocol.
The evaluation protocol is incomplete: the text does not describe the train/test split, folds, or how evaluation negatives were drawn.
User-generated content (text) is not used, and only one classifier family (soft-margin SVM) is tested (Sec. 7, p. 95).
Only two platforms with explicit signed links are studied. Collection period is not stated, and the datasets are older snapshots, so transfer to current platforms is untested.
Recall is defined (Sec. 5.1) but not reported separately; only precision and F1 appear.

summary_md:
Tang, Chang, Aggarwal and Liu (WSDM 2015) ask whether distrust or foe links can be predicted when none are observed, using only positive links and content interactions. They test this on Epinions (14,765 users, 52,704 negative links) and Slashdot (7,275 users, 20,851 negative links). They report three facts. First, negative-link pairs sit close together in the positive network: 82.64% and 87.86% are within 3 hops. Second, signed triads are mostly balanced (92.31% and 93.01%). Third, pairs with negative interactions are far more likely to hold a negative link (t-test p = 5.72e-89 and 1.93e-109). Their SVM, NeLP, adds reliability weights that grow with the interaction count, plus a balance-theory regularizer. Even so, the best F1 on the negative class is only 0.3242 on Epinions and 0.2441 on Slashdot. The simple rule "a negative interaction means a negative link" (negIn) reaches a precision of only 0.2097 and 0.1483. Precision drops the most (-8.70% and -11.08%) when the count-based reliability weights are removed.

For Paul's systems, the paper's main point is a caution. Melange's signed member-reference layer builds negative edges directly from LLM-scored negative references. That is the paper's negIn signal, which the paper shows to be a real but low-precision proxy for an antagonistic relationship. Congress has no explicit foe declaration, so the system cannot score its reference signs against ground truth the way Tang does. Its negative edges should therefore be read as a measure of negative interaction, not of negative ties. The diagnostic signed-coalition partition uses these signs with no evidence-count floor, while the dashboard drawing does use one. The paper's balance statistics support the sign-product logic in the two-hop stance composer. They also give a cheap test the system could run: are negative-reference dyads close together in the cosponsor graph? Every result here comes from 2015-era online trust platforms, not legislatures.

bearings.paper_claim: Negative interactions predict negative links far above chance (t-test p = 5.72e-89 Epinions, 1.93e-109 Slashdot), but as a classifier the rule 'negative interaction implies negative link' (negIn) reaches only precision 0.2097 / F1 0.2826 on Epinions and 0.1483 / 0.1986 on Slashdot. The share of pairs that hold a negative link rises with the number of negative interactions K, and the paper weights each pair's reliability by f(Nij) = 1 - 1/log(1+Nij).
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3.3, pp. 89-90, Fig. 3; Sec. 4.1 Eq. 2; Sec. 5.2 Table 3, p. 93
bearings.system_side: The layer counts an LLM-valenced reference as a signed directed edge. The edge's sign and size come from net = (pos - neg) / substantive contexts. One scored negative context therefore gives net = -1.0, the same as ten unanimous negative contexts. The current member_references.json on disk (read 2026-10-09; denominator = 7,944 directed substantive edges, whole cached corpus) has 1,161 edges with net < 0 and 6,028 with net > 0. These counts come from a single path and are UNVERIFIED. The dashboard draws only edges with n_scored >= 2, but the artifact itself keeps single-context edges.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Tang has ground-truth distrust declarations to score interaction-derived signs against. Congress has no equivalent, so the transferable lesson concerns interpretation, not a calibrated precision figure. A negative reference is evidence of a negative interaction, not a validated antagonistic relationship. The paper's interaction signals are thresholded helpfulness ratings and MPQA comment polarity, a weaker reader than an LLM working on a formality-filtered context. Precision here could be higher or lower, and that is untested. The evidence is strongest for the claim that sign evidence becomes more reliable as the count of contexts grows.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-sna#Co-appearance and signed member-reference layers (display only)|Co-appearance and signed member-reference layers (display only)]]

bearings.paper_claim: Balance holds in 92.31% (Epinions) and 93.01% (Slashdot) of signed triads, which supports balance as a structural constraint. When signs come from interactions rather than declared links, removing the count-based reliability weights cuts precision by 8.70% and 11.08%, and the balance regularizer helps only at small weight (Cb from 0.001 to 0.1). Large Cb hurts.
bearings.system_side: The Aref-Neal frustration-minimizing partition takes sign(net) and weight |net| from member_references.json. MINW defaults to 0.0, and there is no n_scored floor. A one-context negative reference therefore enters with full weight 1.0 and can frustrate the partition as much as a well-evidenced dyad. The output is a diagnostic that the chain does not consume.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Tang's balance figures come from declared trust/distrust networks among online users. The system's signs are interaction-derived, the paper's noisy-label case. Some of the frustration and of the 'splinter' roster may therefore reflect label noise rather than hidden coalitions. A low-cost check that stays within project rules is a diagnostic sensitivity run with the n_scored >= 2 floor the dashboard already uses. The paper does not show what share of the system's frustration is noise.

bearings.paper_claim: Signed triads in two real signed networks are overwhelmingly balanced: 92.31% (Epinions) and 93.01% (Slashdot). Over 9 in 10 triads obey the sign-product rule (the enemy of my enemy is a friend).
bearings.system_side: compose() sets cu_alignment to the product of stance toward a target and the target's CU valence. Support for a CU-positive target counts as support, and opposition to a CU-negative target also counts as support. This is a balance-theory sign product over a speaker, target, CU triad.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's triads are person-to-person trust links. The system's third node is an interest (credit unions), reached through a curated valence registry. The paper gives only a structural prior that sign products usually hold. The system's own measurements bound it more tightly: 0.872 with oracle valence and 0.782 with 5-fold CV of the registry, against a 0.677 flat baseline. The bearing is weak, and it does not validate the registry.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Two-hop stance x valence decomposition with curated registry|Two-hop stance x valence decomposition with curated registry]]

bearings.paper_claim: With negative-to-missing imbalance of 1:4131 and 1:2534, accuracy misleads: a trivial classifier can reach 99.99%. The paper therefore reports precision and F1 on the rare class. It also reports parameterized baselines at their best setting and tunes NeLP per site, without a held-out tuning protocol.
bearings.system_side: The forecaster is scored on rare positive joins using AUC, average precision and bill-averaged precision@10/25/50. It is compared against named baselines (B1 member propensity) with average precision as the comparison metric, never accuracy. The forecast is frozen before scoring.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This bears on the choice of metric only, which carries across domains. Tang's best-setting baseline reporting and per-site tuning are what the system's frozen, single-look scoring is built to avoid. The paper is a negative example on protocol, not a template.

gaps_exposed: No evidence-count reliability on signed reference edges. net = (pos-neg)/sub treats a single scored context the same as many unanimous ones, and signed_coalitions.py applies no n_scored floor. Only the dashboard drawing filters at n_scored >= 2.

No ground truth for negative ties. The system cannot estimate the precision of LLM-valenced negative references as relationship indicators. Tang's negIn precision (0.15-0.21) shows that this gap matters.

A cheap untested check: Tang's 'enemies are close' pattern (82.64% and 87.86% of negative pairs within 3 hops of the positive graph) could be measured for negative-reference dyads on the cosponsor graph. The result would show whether negative references sit inside working relationships or across camps.

Signed triad census not reported: the share of balanced triads in member_references.json is not measured. That share would show how much of the Aref-Neal frustration is structural and how much is label noise.

Negative signs never enter the cascade kernel. Out-party sources get a cpf_pressure of 0.5 rather than a negative edge. The paper argues that negative links add value, but this project has not tested that for Congress.
flags: NEAR-REJECTED PROPOSAL: Tang's count-based reliability weight f(Nij) = 1 - 1/log(1+Nij) is a form of per-edge evidence-volume weighting. Per-edge volume normalization was measured and REJECTED in this project. Do not recommend reweighting cascade or SNA edges by volume on this paper's authority. At most, apply the existing n_scored >= 2 floor as a diagnostic sensitivity run on signed_coalitions.

Status theory (94.73% and 93.38% status-consistent triads) concerns directional asymmetry in declared links. It must not be read as evidence for reciprocity, which is NOT validated in this system (D-104..D-108).
The edge counts quoted here (7,944 directed edges, 1,161 with net < 0, as of 2026-10-09 on disk) come from one read path and stay UNVERIFIED until reproduced by a second path (DE-062).
Negative references and signed-partition outputs must not be described as measured hostility, closeness or access (D-025). They are model outputs built on LLM-valenced interactions.
paul_alignment: Paul's position for co-appearance-and-references is that LLM valence per context window answers his question about negative ties. Tang supports this only in part. Negative interactions carry strong signal about negative relationships, but as a direct label they are noisy (negIn precision 0.21 on Epinions and 0.15 on Slashdot), and reliability grows with the number of interactions. The system therefore measures negative interactions, not validated negative ties. Paul's note reads the layer more strongly than this evidence allows, and it does not mention that the diagnostic signed partition uses single-context edges at full weight. For two-hop decomposition, Paul asked how agreement is quantified when two actors share negative sentiment toward a third. Tang's balance census (about 92-93% balanced triads) is direct supporting evidence for the sign-product answer the system already uses in compose(), though from online trust networks rather than Congress. For signed coalitions, the paper supports Paul's interest in Aref-Neal balance partitions but adds the caveat about noisy labels.

related.why: Tang reuses Leskovec et al.'s 16 weighted signed-triad features and signed-link setting, then extends them to the case where no negative links are observed.

Aref and Neal partition a signed House network by generalized balance, the method signed_coalitions.py implements. Tang's balance census and noisy-label results bear on how far that partition can be trusted when signs come from interactions.

This is the same frustration-minimization approach applied to signed political collaboration. Tang supplies the balance-prevalence evidence that motivates it and the caution about interaction-derived signs.
Both are link-prediction papers built on neighbourhood and similarity features. Zareie predicts positive links, and Tang adds the signed and negative-link case.

extraction.title: Adversarial Attack on Graph Neural Networks as an Influence Maximization Problem
extraction.venue: WSDM 2022 (Fifteenth ACM International Conference on Web Search and Data Mining), Tempe AZ, virtual, Research Paper track, pp. 675-685
extraction.document_type: Conference paper (WSDM 2022 research paper, 11 pages including references and appendices)
extraction.coverage: Read the full text file in chunks: lines 1-1391 and 1392-1699 (all of it), covering abstract, introduction, related work, preliminaries, Section 4 analysis (4.1-4.4, Propositions 1-2, Lemma 1, Corollaries 1-2), Section 5 experiments (Tables 1-3, Figures 2-3), conclusion, references 1-35, and Appendices A (proofs) and B (additional experiments). Metadata hint verified: title, venue, year and DOI are correct; authors confirmed from the header. Paul markup: no markup files were listed for this document, and no annotation file named d3f0c986a967.json exists in the research _annots folder (checked by filename only; the other 63 annotation files were not opened), so paul_markup is empty. Scope note: the paper has no material on lobbying, elections, persuasion or turnout, legislators, or text measurement. Network content is graph influence (linear threshold model), random-walk importance and centrality baselines.
extraction.research_question: Can a restricted, realistic black-box attack on a GNN, which perturbs the features of a small set of nodes with no access to model parameters or predictions, be formalized and solved efficiently by connecting node selection to influence maximization on a threshold model? (Abstract; Sections 1 and 3.2, pp. 675-677.)
extraction.theory: Adversarial attack on GNNs recast as influence maximization. Under a ReLU path-independence assumption (Assumption 1, after Xu et al. 2018), the expected mis-classification rate becomes a spread function on a directed bipartite graph with node-specific thresholds (general or linear threshold model, Kempe et al. 2003). The objective is submodular when threshold CDFs are concave on the positive domain (Proposition 2, p. 678), so greedy selection applies. Section 4.2, p. 677-678.
extraction.data: Three public citation benchmarks: Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed (Sen et al. 2008; Yang et al. 2016). Unit: nodes. Graph sizes N are not stated in the text. Random 60/20/20 train/validation/test splits (Table 1 and 2); 10 percent training data in Table 3 and Appendix B.2. 40 independent trials per model-dataset pair. Victim models: GCN and GAT with 2 layers, JK-Net with 7 layers. Proxy models: 20 GCNs trained on separate splits to build the perturbation vector. Period: not stated; benchmark data only, no time period.
extraction.method: Two-step attack: (1) select a node set S with |S| at most r and degree at most m; (2) add a constant perturbation vector epsilon to features of nodes in S. The paper focuses on step 1. InfMax-Unif greedily maximizes the saturated coverage objective h(S) = sum over j of (min(sum over i in S of B_ji, a) + b) divided by (a+b), with B = M^L (random-walk transition matrix, L = 4), uniform threshold distribution, a = 0.01 (Corollary 1, Eq. 6). InfMax-Norm greedily maximizes sum over j of (1 + erf(sum B_ji / (sigma sqrt 2)))/2 with sigma = 0.01 (Corollary 2, Eq. 7). Baselines: Degree, Betweenness, PageRank (alpha = 0.85), RWCS and GC-RWCS (Ma et al. 2020; L = 4, l = 30, k = 1). Constraints: r = 1 percent of graph size; m = lowest degree of the top 10 or 30 percent of nodes. Perturbation: lambda = 10, top 2 percent features by average gradient sign-consistent across 20 proxy GCNs, value in {-lambda, 0, lambda}. Significance: pairwise t-test at alpha 0.05. Section 3.2 and 5.1-5.2, pp. 676-681.
extraction.identification: Not applicable in the causal sense. This is an adversarial-attack benchmark, not causal inference. Validity rests on the black-box design: proxy GCNs trained on different splits build the perturbation vector, so it does not depend on victim models. The authors note the Ma et al. 2020 setup used victim-model information (Appendix B.1).
extraction.scope: Population: node-level, untargeted, evasion, black-box attacks by feature perturbation on GNNs (GCN, GAT, JK-Net) for node classification on three citation networks. Institution: University of Michigan School of Information. Era: 2022 publication on 2008-2016 public benchmarks. Excludes graph-topology perturbation and binary or nonnegative features (future work, p. 685).

limitations: Assumption 1 (ReLU activations independent with a common probability) is an approximation taken from Xu et al. 2018; it is a simplification of the real network.

The thresholds are treated as random. The authors say independence across nodes is unrealistic for GNNs because neighbours' predictions correlate, and they leave concentration of the mis-classification rate around its expectation to future work (Section 4.4, p. 679).
The distribution assumptions (uniform or normal thresholds) likely deviate from the real distribution; the authors state this (p. 679).
Hyperparameters a and sigma are fixed at 0.01 without tuning; the theoretically optimal choice depends on epsilon and the dataset (p. 679).
Only node selection is studied. The perturbation vector is constant across nodes (no personalization), and the attack is untargeted.
Only feature perturbation with continuous features is treated; graph-structure perturbation and binary or nonnegative features are future work (Conclusion, p. 685).
The bipartite connection uses rho (the path activation probability), which is unknown; visualization sets rho = 1 (footnote 5, p. 681).
Evaluation covers three citation benchmarks and three GNN architectures with a single attack budget r = 1 percent of graph size. Graph sizes are not reported in the text.
Greedy submodularity gives an approximation guarantee for the expected objective, not for the actual mis-classification rate. The paper does not prove the concentration of the actual rate.

summary_md:
Ma, Deng and Mei (WSDM 2022) study a strict black-box attack on graph neural networks. The attacker cannot see model parameters or predictions. It may change the features of at most r nodes (1 percent of the graph), each with degree at most m. The paper's main contribution is choosing which nodes to perturb. Under a ReLU path-independence approximation, the expected misclassification rate becomes an influence-maximization objective on a directed bipartite linear-threshold graph. Influence weights are B = M^L (an L-step random walk, L = 4), and the thresholds are random. The problem is NP-hard (Lemma 1). It is submodular, so greedy selection carries a guarantee, only when each threshold CDF is concave on the positive domain (Proposition 2). Uniform thresholds give a saturated-coverage objective (InfMax-Unif) and normal thresholds give an erf objective (InfMax-Norm). On Cora, Citeseer and Pubmed, both methods usually cut test accuracy more than the GC-RWCS, PageRank, degree and betweenness baselines; degree and betweenness are the weakest. One example is Cora GAT: 87.7 with no attack, 57.5 under GC-RWCS and 55.9 under InfMax-Unif. Near-ties occur on Citeseer. A qualitative SBM case study suggests the better selectors spread their seeds across communities.

The paper does not concern legislatures, lobbying or persuasion, so nothing about political behavior transfers. What does transfer is the mathematics. Proposition 2 gives the exact condition for a greedy guarantee on a threshold model: the threshold CDF must be concave. Paul's system uses deterministic tier thresholds in lt_priming and lazy greedy over Monte Carlo spread in the frontier and coalition allocators. The paper says when those greedy claims hold and when they do not. Its other lessons are that coverage-style saturating objectives beat raw centrality, and that seed sets should avoid redundancy. The adversarial result itself has no counterpart in the system, which runs no GNN. It does give an analogy for testing how neighbour-propagated stance imputation behaves when a few node inputs are corrupted. That analogy is weak and UNVERIFIED.

bearings.paper_claim: In a general or linear threshold model with random node thresholds, the expected spread h(S) is submodular when every threshold CDF F_j is concave on [0, inf) (Proposition 2). Without that condition, linear-threshold influence maximization on the bipartite graph is NP-hard (Lemma 1, by reduction from Set Cover). Uniform thresholds give the submodular saturated-coverage objective sum_j (min(sum_i B_ji, a) + b)/(a+b) (Corollary 1, Eq. 6).
bearings.paper_location: Section 4.2-4.3, Lemma 1, Proposition 2, Corollary 1, pp. 678-679; proof Appendix A.2
bearings.system_side: lt_priming uses a linear-threshold adoption rule with DETERMINISTIC thresholds: a fixed tier ladder THETA (Highly Persuadable 0.6 up to Opponent 3.0), plus a lean term and +COMMIT per Opponent cell. Pressure is the sum of kernel probabilities from active pro neighbours. Each target is solved separately for the cheapest mix of recruits and money, and no seed-set guarantee is claimed.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the mathematics transfers; the GNN and citation-benchmark context does not. A point-mass threshold has a step CDF, which is not concave, so any future step that aggregates lt_priming targets into a seed-set objective and then cites a (1-1/e) greedy bound would be unsupported. Randomizing theta by tier (for example, uniform around the ladder value) would make the bound available, at the cost of an unestimated spread parameter. The per-target cheapest-tip solve is unaffected. Moderate for the mathematical condition, weak for empirical relevance.

bearings.paper_claim: Selectors that account for overlap in coverage (InfMax-Unif and InfMax-Norm through saturation, and GC-RWCS) beat selectors that rank nodes by stand-alone importance (degree, betweenness, PageRank). In Table 1 the proposed methods beat all baselines in all but 3 of 18 setups (authors' count); for example, Pubmed GAT at the 30% threshold gives 64.1 vs 69.1 for GC-RWCS (85.2 with no attack). In an SBM with 4 communities, the better selectors spread seeds more evenly across communities (Figure 3, qualitative, no statistic).
bearings.paper_location: Section 5.2 Table 1, pp. 680-681; Section 5.4 Figure 3, p. 681
bearings.system_side: The coalition allocator ranks the top-45 neutral candidates by SINGLETON marginal spread({n}) - base. It boosts that by (1 + 0.8 bpf) and water-fills $2M in proportion. Redundancy among funded seeds enters only through the joint spread reported afterwards; it never shapes the selection.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's objective is GNN misclassification on citation graphs at a 1% node budget. The CU objective is a Monte Carlo competitive cascade on the cosponsor kernel. The transferable point is structural: ranking by singleton marginals ignores overlap, so funded seeds can cluster in one community. The code already measures the joint-vs-naive gap ('naive-additive'). Comparing the singleton-marginal set against a lazy-greedy set (budget_frontier already implements one) would show whether the gap matters. The paper's community-spread finding is qualitative. Weak to moderate.

bearings.paper_claim: A saturated, coverage-style objective over L-step random-walk influence B = M^L (L = 4) is submodular and outperforms one-step and centrality heuristics. Influence is counted over multi-hop walks with a cap per receiver (a = 0.01), not over direct ties.
bearings.paper_location: Corollary 1 Eq. 6, Section 4.3, p. 678-679; Section 5.1 settings, p. 679
bearings.system_side: budgetRecruit performs cost-bounded max-coverage greedy with cov[v] = 1 - prod(1 - p) over the selected recruiters' DIRECT edge probabilities. It claims (1-1/e) through monotone submodular coverage, with GCOMB-style locality and degree pruning. Coverage is one hop.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports a saturating coverage surrogate as a well-founded submodular stand-in for threshold spread, and it independently backs the existing (1-1/e) claim for this mode. The extension is multi-hop coverage: replace p with an L-step walk-weighted reach on the kernel. On the cosponsor graph, M would be the degree-normalized kernel, so the result is a heuristic reach score (D-025), not an introduction probability. It must not become per-edge volume normalization, which was REJECTED. Weak.

bearings.paper_claim: As seed selectors, plain centralities are weaker than random-walk column sums with saturation. In Table 1, Degree and Betweenness fall below RWCS, GC-RWCS and InfMax, and PageRank (alpha 0.85) is intermediate. Random-walk column sum I(i) = sum_j [M^L]_ji is the importance measure behind the strongest baseline.
bearings.paper_location: Section 5.1 baselines and Section 5.2 Table 1, pp. 679-681
bearings.system_side: kb_benchmark computes Katz-Bonacich centrality, b = (I - dA)^-1 1 with delta = 0.85/lambda_max, on the live kernel P = build_P(adj). It counts weighted out-walks, and is used only as a Spearman diagnostic against allocations, money and the legislative score; the chain never consumes it.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Katz-Bonacich is a walk-sum importance measure close to RWCS (unnormalized and infinite-horizon rather than L = 4). The paper's evidence that unsaturated walk sums leave value on the table, relative to coverage-aware selection, fits the system's choice to keep KB diagnostic only. The paper concerns attack selection on GNN benchmarks, not legislators, so this is context only, and KB scores remain heuristic outputs (D-025).

bearings.paper_claim: Perturbing the features of only 1% of nodes, chosen by an influence-maximization criterion, sharply lowers the accuracy of graph-propagating predictors (GCN, GAT, JK-Net). An example is Cora GAT, which falls from 87.7 to 55.9 at the 10% degree threshold. Propagation through the graph is what lets a few nodes affect many predictions.
bearings.system_side: Neighbour imputation proposes a tier for a silent (member, issue) cell from the mean TSCORE of at least 5 labelled cosponsor neighbours, kept when |est| >= 0.75. Masking validation reports about 77% sign agreement. These are proposals only; the matrix is unchanged.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The system has no GNN. It uses a one-hop mean and a human-adjudicated output, so propagation is shallow and an adversary is implausible. The transferable idea is a robustness check: perturb or flip the labels of a few high-coverage members, chosen by walk-coverage rather than at random, and measure how many proposals change sign. That would separate label-error sensitivity from the 77% agreement figure. Weak; any result is UNVERIFIED until reproduced (DE-062).

gaps_exposed: No greedy step states whether its objective is submodular. budget_frontier and per_topic_coalition run lazy greedy or marginal ranking over a competitive cascade with bystander activation. The paper shows that a guarantee needs a specific structural condition (concave threshold CDF), so a (1-1/e) bound should not be assumed from greedy alone.
lt_priming's thresholds are deterministic tier constants. A seed-set version of LT priming would have no greedy guarantee, and NP-hardness applies (Lemma 1).

The coalition allocator funds by singleton marginals and checks redundancy only afterwards (joint vs naive-additive). There is no overlap-aware selection like that of the coverage-objective methods, which beat stand-alone-importance baselines.
There is no robustness test of graph-propagated estimates (neighbour imputation, cascade spreads) against a few corrupted or mislabelled high-coverage nodes.
Coverage in budgetRecruit is one hop. Multi-hop, saturating reach has not been tried.
flags: The paper's 'influence' means spread of misclassification in a GNN. It is not legislator influence, and its results must not be quoted as evidence about persuasion, lobbying or access.
Random-walk importance B = M^L and walk-sum centralities are heuristic model outputs, never closeness, access or introduction probabilities (D-025).

Porting M = D^-1 A to the cosponsor graph normalizes by node degree. Check that it does not bring back the REJECTED per-edge volume-normalization proposal under another name. The paper itself argues for neither rejected SNA proposal.
Table 1 figures come from 3 citation benchmarks, 40 trials and a 1% node budget, with no graph sizes reported. Any number quoted must carry that window and denominator.
The paper's count of 'all but 3 of 18 setups' was not independently rechecked, and Citeseer at the 10% threshold shows near-ties.
paul_alignment: The paper sharpens Paul's own caution. His margin note on Chen 2023 says pressure from high-ranking members is "not diminishing", which he reads as a challenge to submodular assumptions. Proposition 2 makes that exact: the greedy guarantee holds only when the threshold CDF is concave. Non-diminishing or step-like threshold responses break it. Paul's three-tier architecture places the per-topic allocators in a "static and submodular" tier. As built, those allocators run greedy over a competitive cascade with bystander mobilization, and the code never establishes submodularity. Labelling that tier submodular is therefore an assumption, not a property. His GCOMB and CELF expectations for the joint optimizer are untouched, because that optimizer is separable and concave per member. Paul has no annotation on this paper.

related.why: Complex contagion is the non-concave-threshold case where Proposition 2's submodularity fails. The two papers together bound when greedy seeding is justified.
Competitive LT models can lose submodularity, which the flip model already cites. Ma et al. give the single-campaign condition (concave CDF) under which it is recovered.
Both rely on the submodularity-implies-greedy-guarantee result. Ma et al. derive submodularity from the threshold distribution, the property Golovin and Krause assume.

Almazaydeh argues centrality heuristics rival greedy in influence maximization. Ma et al. find degree, betweenness and PageRank weaker than greedy on a coverage objective, though in a GNN-attack setting.
Both connect GNNs and influence maximization in opposite directions: Kumar uses GNNs to solve influence maximization, and Ma et al. use influence maximization to attack GNNs.
If a temporal GNN stance model is adopted, the restricted black-box node-perturbation vulnerability shown here becomes a direct robustness concern.
